text: preferred for infections with C. lusitaniae. Amphotericin B is used for other non-albicans infections, although there is some evidence of resistance developing in C. krusei and C. gla- brata. However, these species are susceptible to voricona- zole and caspofungin and voriconazole may also be used as an alternative for fluconazole-resistant invasive Candi- da infections.1 Neonates with disseminated candidiasis are usually best treated with amphotericin B, although fluco- nazole may also be effective.1,10 Empirical antifungal therapy may be appropriate for neu- tropenic patients. Drugs that may be considered include amphotericin B, itraconazole, or voriconazole. Flucona- zole is unsuitable because of its restricted antifungal spec- trum. The role of caspofungin is uncertain.1 Treatment should generally be continued until signs and symptoms have resolved and the patient is no longer neutropenic. For empirical antifungal treatment in non-neutropenic pa- tients, amphotericin B or fluconazole may be considered.1 Although antifungal prophylaxis is generally not routinely recommended for non-neutropenic patients, some would consider it appropriate in patients who are at high risk of infection such as patients who are critically ill, neutropen- ic, or receiving solid organ or bone marrow transplants.1,11 1.
